docs.title: 1. Why version control, and why doubly now
docs.text:
You have already invented version control, badly: memoire_v2.docx, memoire_v2_final.docx, memoire_v2_final_REAL.docx. Git is the same idea done properly. You keep working on the same files; Git keeps every snapshot you ask it to keep, with a date, an author, and a message, and can show you the difference between any two of them or bring any of them back.

For your own work, that gives you:

  • an undo button that reaches back weeks, not seconds;
  • the freedom to try something risky, because the working version is one command away;
  • a history that explains why the code looks the way it does.

For work done by an AI coding agent — Sessions 3 and 4 — this stops being comfort and becomes safety. An agent edits ten files in thirty seconds. Without git you cannot see what it touched, you cannot tell its good edits from its bad ones, and you cannot go back. With git, every one of those edits is a diff you can read and a commit you can revert. Two rules you will apply from Session 4 on:

Rules of the agent era

  1. Commit before you let an agent touch the repository. A clean working tree is the state you can always return to.
  2. git diff is how you review what it did. Not the agent's summary of what it did — the diff.

An agent without git is a liability. That is the whole reason this session comes first.

docs.title: 2. The mental model: three places, one history
docs.text:
Git does not track a file. It tracks a folder (a repository, or repo), as a series of snapshots you choose to take. Each snapshot is a commit. Think of three places your work can be:

 your files on disk        the staging area          the history (.git)
 ("working tree")          ("index", a loading dock)  (commits, permanent)

   edit files  ───git add───▶  chosen changes  ───git commit───▶  snapshot #7
                                                                  snapshot #6
       ◀───────────────────── git restore ────────────────────    snapshot #5
                                                                      ...
  • Working tree — the normal files you edit with any editor.
  • Staging area — where you put the changes you want in the next commit. This extra step is deliberate: you often have three unrelated edits in a folder and want to commit only the finished one.
  • History — the commits, stored in a hidden folder called .git at the root of the repo. Delete .git and the history is gone; the folder goes back to being plain files.

A commit records the whole folder as it was at that moment, not "what changed". (Git is clever about storage, but the model you should carry is snapshot, not diff.) Each commit has a permanent identifier, its hash — a 40-character hexadecimal string, of which you will only ever type the first seven.

Reference for the curious: Pro Git §1.3, "What is Git?".

docs.title: 3. One-time configuration
docs.text:
Git stamps your name and email on every commit. Set them once; this is global to your machine. The last two lines avoid two classic traps: new repositories are still created with a branch called master unless told otherwise (GitHub and this course use main), and git commit without a message opens an editor — we make that editor nano, which is the one you can exit.

Any terminal (WSL / Mac / Git Bash / Codespace)
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@etu.unistra.fr"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor nano

Use the same email as your GitHub account, so GitHub attributes your commits to you. Check:

Any terminal
git config --global --list

Expected: four lines, user.name=..., user.email=..., init.defaultbranch=main, core.editor=nano.

docs.title: 4. Hands-on: a website under version control
docs.text: We practise on a tiny website — three HTML pages and one stylesheet — because a web page makes Git visible: change a file, refresh the browser, see the change; go back in history, refresh, see the old version. You do not need to know HTML; you will only ever change a word or a number.

docs.title: 4.1 Get the files
docs.text:
Go to your home folder and download the site. The second command downloads a compressed archive and unpacks it in one go (| sends the output of curl into tar; xz means extract a gzip-compressed archive).

Any terminal
# If the curl line fails: download https://knuxv.github.io/cours-agents/files/practice-site.zip
# in your browser, unzip it (double-click), and cd into the practice-site folder it contains.
cd ~
curl -L https://knuxv.github.io/cours-agents/files/practice-site.tar.gz | tar xz
cd practice-site
ls

Expected: about.html contact.html index.html style.css. (Downloads: practice-site.zip · practice-site.tar.gz. The four files are also browsable here and in the course repository under site/docs/files/practice-site/.)

If you unzipped by hand on Windows

The folder is probably in Downloads. From WSL, that is cd /mnt/c/Users/<YourWindowsName>/Downloads/practice-site; from Git Bash, cd ~/Downloads/practice-site. Better: move the folder to your home first (see where to keep your work).

Open the page in your browser:

WSLMacGit BashCodespaces Ubuntu window (WSL)
explorer.exe index.html
Terminal (Mac)
open index.html
Git Bash
start index.html

There is no local browser. Serve the folder and use the Open in Browser button that pops up:

Codespace terminal (browser)
python3 -m http.server 8000

Press Ctrl+C to stop the server when you need the terminal back.

You see "Riverside Coding Club", a navigation bar, a tagline, and a "Next meetup" box. Keep this browser tab open.

docs.title: 4.2 git init — start tracking
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside practice-site
git init
ls -a
git status
  • git init creates the hidden .git folder. ls -a shows it (the -a shows hidden files, whose names start with a dot).
  • git status is the command you will run most. Right now it lists the four files as untracked: Git sees them but is not recording anything about them yet.

Ran git init in the wrong folder?

Check with pwd before running it. If you did it somewhere else (your home folder, typically), remove the stray .git there — rm -rf ~/.git if it was your home folder — and redo it inside practice-site. A .git in your home folder makes every folder on your machine look like part of one giant repository.

docs.title: 4.3 git add, git commit — the first snapshot
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside practice-site
git add .
git status
git commit -m "Initial commit of the club website"
git status
  • git add . puts every file in the current folder (.) on the loading dock. The second git status now says Changes to be committed.
  • git commit -m "..." seals the dock into a snapshot. The -m gives the message inline; always use -m in this course.
  • The last git status says nothing to commit, working tree clean: every file on disk matches the last snapshot.

docs.title: 4.4 Edit, look, commit — the everyday cycle
docs.text:
Open index.html in an editor (nano index.html or micro index.html in the terminal, or VS Code — see Editing files if you are on WSL). Find the line

<p>Tuesday, 7:00 PM, Room B12.</p>

change 7:00 to 7:30, save (in nano: Ctrl+O, Enter, then Ctrl+X), and refresh the browser tab: the new time is on the page. Now ask Git what it thinks:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git status
git diff

git status says index.html is modified, not staged. git diff shows the change: a line starting with - (removed) and one starting with + (added). Press q if the output opens in a pager. This is the reviewing habit: look at the diff before you commit.

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git add index.html
git diff
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Move meetup time to 7:30 PM"

Note what happened in the middle: after git add, plain git diff shows nothing (there is no unstaged change left), and git diff --staged shows the change waiting on the dock. Same edit, different question.

Commit messages

Write the message as an instruction, in the imperative: "Move meetup time to 7:30 PM", not "moved" or "I changed the time". Read it as "if applied, this commit will ⟨message⟩". One logical change per commit: if you fixed a colour and corrected a sentence, that is two commits, so that either can be undone alone. (Full argument: How to Write a Git Commit Message. In Session 4 you will put these rules in your AGENTS.md so the agent follows them too.)

docs.title: 4.5 git log, git show — read the history
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside practice-site
git log
git log --oneline

git log lists commits newest first with hash, author, date and message (press q to quit). --oneline is the compact view you will use most: one line per commit, seven-character hash on the left. Now inspect one commit — pick the hash of "Move meetup time" from the --oneline output:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git show <hash>

git show prints that commit's message and its diff: git log and git diff aimed at a single commit. Without a hash it shows the most recent commit.

docs.title: 4.6 git restore — the undo button
docs.text:
Three levels of undo, from the harmless to the one that deletes work.

Discard an edit you have not committed. Open about.html, delete an entire section, save. Then:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git status
git restore about.html
git status

The file is back to the last committed version. Refresh the browser to confirm. This one has no undo: the deleted edit was never committed, so Git has no copy of it. Only use it on changes you are sure you want to throw away.

Unstage without losing the edit. Change the email address in contact.html, then stage it too early:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git add contact.html
git status
git restore --staged contact.html
git status

The edit is still in the file; it is just off the dock again. (Then either commit it or git restore contact.html to drop it.)

Bring back a whole file from an old commit. Delete a file for real, then recover it from history:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
rm style.css
ls
git status
git restore style.css
ls

Refresh the browser in between: without style.css the page loses its styling; after git restore it is back. To pull a file from a commit older than the last one, add --source:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git restore --source=<hash> index.html
git diff

Notice that nothing was rewritten: you now have an old version of one file as an uncommitted change. You can commit it forward (a new commit whose content matches an old one) or git restore index.html to go back to the latest. "Going back" in Git almost always means making a new commit, not erasing history.

You will see git checkout everywhere

Before 2019, one command, git checkout, did both "discard this file's changes" and "switch branch". git checkout -- about.html is the old form of git restore about.html. This course uses restore and switch, which cannot be confused with each other; just recognise checkout in older tutorials and in what agents write.

docs.title: 4.7 .gitignore — what never goes in history
docs.text:
Some files live in the project folder but should not be tracked: scratch notes, editor backups, .venv (Session 2), .env files with secrets (Session 2). Create a scratch file and see Git offer to track it, then tell it not to:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
echo "todo: fix the tagline" > notes.txt
git status
echo "notes.txt" > .gitignore
git status
git add .gitignore
git commit -m "Ignore local scratch notes"

notes.txt is still on disk and still yours; it simply disappeared from git status. The .gitignore file itself is committed: it is a rule about the project, shared with anyone who clones it.

docs.title: 5.1 A branch is a pointer
docs.text:
A branch is not a copy of your project. It is a named pointer to a commit, and HEAD is Git's note of which branch you are on. main is the branch you have been on since git init. Right now the practice site looks like this (arrows go forward in time; each circle is a commit):

flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C))
    main[main]:::branch -.-> C
    HEAD[HEAD]:::head -.-> main
    classDef branch fill:#e8eaf6,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#1a237e
    classDef head fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ef6c00,color:#e65100

Creating a branch adds a second pointer at the same commit. Nothing is copied, nothing is slow — which is why people create a branch for every experiment and every task.

docs.title: 5.2 Create, commit, switch
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside practice-site
git branch
git switch -c bigger-welcome

git branch lists branches (one, main, marked *). git switch -c creates a branch and moves HEAD onto it. Now edit index.html: change the "Welcome" heading to "Welcome!" and add a sentence to the paragraph below it. Save, refresh the browser, then:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git add index.html
git commit -m "Make the welcome section friendlier"
git log --oneline --all --graph

The commit moved bigger-welcome forward; main stayed where it was:

flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> D((D))
    main[main]:::branch -.-> C
    bw[bigger-welcome]:::branch -.-> D
    HEAD[HEAD]:::head -.-> bw
    classDef branch fill:#e8eaf6,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#1a237e
    classDef head fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ef6c00,color:#e65100

Switch back and watch your files change:

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git switch main            # refresh the browser: the edit is gone
git switch bigger-welcome  # refresh: it is back

Nothing was deleted. Switching branches replaces your working files with whatever the branch's latest commit says they should be; main's commit C simply never contained your edit.

docs.title: 5.3 Case 1: main has not moved — fast-forward
docs.text:
Merges happen from the branch you are merging into. Go back to main and merge:

Any terminal, inside practice-site — on main
git switch main
git merge bigger-welcome
git log --oneline --all --graph

Git prints Fast-forward. main had no commit of its own since the branch was created, so D is a straight continuation of C: Git just moves the main pointer up to D. No new commit is created; the two names now point at the same place.

flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> D((D))
    main[main]:::branch -.-> D
    bw[bigger-welcome]:::branch -.-> D
    classDef branch fill:#e8eaf6,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#1a237e

The branch has done its job; delete the pointer (the commit stays):

Any terminal, inside practice-site
git branch -d bigger-welcome

docs.title: 5.4 Case 2: main has moved — a merge commit
docs.text:
Now the realistic case: while you work on a branch, main receives a commit of its own (a colleague's, an agent's, or yours from another task). Create a branch, commit on it, then go back to main and commit there too:

Any terminal, inside practice-site — on main
git switch -c footer-year

Edit the <footer> line of index.html to read © 2026 Riverside Coding Club, then:

Any terminal, inside practice-site — on footer-year
git add index.html
git commit -m "Add the year to the footer"
git switch main

Now, on main, change the email address in contact.html, and:

Any terminal, inside practice-site — on main
git add contact.html
git commit -m "Update the contact email"
git log --oneline --all --graph

The history has forked. Each branch has a commit the other does not have:

flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> D((D))
    D --> E((E))
    D --> F((F))
    main[main]:::branch -.-> E
    fy[footer-year]:::branch -.-> F
    classDef branch fill:#e8eaf6,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#1a237e

Merge anyway:

Any terminal, inside practice-site — on main
git merge footer-year

An editor opens with a proposed message, Merge branch 'footer-year' — save and quit (nano: Ctrl+X, then Y if asked, Enter). This time Git could not just move a pointer: main had E, the branch had F, and neither contains the other. So Git made a merge commit M, a snapshot combining both, with two parents:

flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> D((D))
    D --> E((E)) --> M((M))
    D --> F((F)) --> M
    main[main]:::branch -.-> M
    fy[footer-year]:::branch -.-> F
    classDef branch fill:#e8eaf6,stroke:#3f51b5,color:#1a237e
Any terminal, inside practice-site
git log --oneline --graph
git branch -d footer-year

git log --graph now draws the diamond. Refresh the browser: both the year and the new email are there. Git merged the two files automatically because the two commits touched different lines. The one rule to remember: fast-forward if the target has not moved, merge commit if it has.

docs.title: 5.5 Case 3: both sides changed the same line — conflict
docs.text:
Same setup as case 2, except that both commits edit the same line. Git cannot know which version is right, so it stops halfway and asks you:

flowchart LR
    A((A)) --> B((B)) --> C((C)) --> D((D))
    D --> E((E<br/>tagline v1))
    D --> F((F<br/>tagline v2))
    E -.-> X{{CONFLICT}}:::conflict
    F -.-> X
    classDef conflict fill:#ffebee,stroke:#c62828,color:#b71c1c
Auto-merging index.html
CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html
Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

Open the file: Git has written both versions into it, between markers.

<<<<<<< HEAD
<p class="tagline">We build weird little projects.</p>
=======
<p class="tagline">Come build weird little projects with us — all levels welcome.</p>
>>>>>>> friendlier-tagline
  • Between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======: the version on the branch you are on (main).
  • Between ======= and >>>>>>>: the version from the branch being merged.

Resolving a conflict is three steps, and none of them is a Git trick: edit the file so that it contains what you want (one version, the other, or a mix — and delete the three marker lines), git add it to tell Git "resolved", git commit to finish the merge. git status lists the conflicted files at every step; git merge --abort throws the whole attempt away if you get lost.

You will do exactly this on a real Python project in exercise 1.2, where two branches add a language to the same dictionary. Conflicts are not failures: they are Git refusing to guess.

Seeing it move

Learn Git Branching, first sequence, five minutes: every command above, animated on the graph.

docs.title: 6. The deliverable: your course repository
docs.text: You will spend Sessions 2–4 inside one repository, and the agent harness of Session 4 expects to run inside a git repo — this is not busy-work. Name it agent-lab. (Not cours-agents: that is the name of the course's own repository, and the two side by side on your disk will confuse you and us.)

docs.title: 6.1 Create it locally
docs.text:
Any terminal
cd ~
mkdir agent-lab
cd agent-lab
git init
echo "# agent-lab — Advanced Programming for Economists" > README.md
echo "Your Name — M2, 2026" >> README.md
printf ".venv/\n.env\n__pycache__/\n" > .gitignore
git add README.md .gitignore
git commit -m "Initial commit"

The .gitignore already contains the three things Session 2 must never commit: the virtual environment, secret files, Python's cache.

docs.title: 6.2 Log in to GitHub from the terminal, once
docs.text:
GitHub does not accept your account password from git. We use the GitHub CLI, gh, which logs you in through the browser once and lets git reuse that login afterwards.

WSL (Ubuntu)MacGit BashCodespaces Ubuntu window (WSL)
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y gh
gh auth login

Download and run the macOS installer (.pkg) from cli.github.com, then:

Terminal (Mac)
gh auth login

(With Homebrew: brew install gh.)

Nothing to install: Git for Windows bundles a credential manager. The first git push below opens a browser window asking you to sign in to GitHub; approve it and the push completes. Skip gh auth login.

Nothing to do: gh is preinstalled and logged in (gh auth status).

gh auth login asks a few questions. Answer GitHub.com → HTTPS → Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes → Login with a web browser. It shows a one-time code; press Enter; a browser opens on github.com/login/device (if nothing opens — typical in WSL — open that address yourself in your Windows browser). Type the code, approve. The terminal prints Logged in as <your-username>. If this fails in class, a personal access token generated on GitHub, pasted as the password when git push asks for one, is the fallback — come and see us.

docs.title: 6.3 Publish it
docs.text:
On github.com: + (top right) → New repository → name agent-lab → leave every checkbox unchecked (no README, no .gitignore, no licence) → Create repository. Your local repository already has a history; an empty remote simply receives it. Copy the HTTPS URL shown, then:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/agent-lab.git
git remote -v
git push -u origin main

origin is the conventional name for "the copy on GitHub" — the Session 1½ reading explains remotes properly. -u ties your local main to it, so that from now on plain git push and git pull know where to go. Refresh the GitHub page: your README is there.

Done when

https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/agent-lab shows your README, and git status in the folder says working tree clean. Bring this folder to Session 2. (If you did Session 0 on Codespaces: create the repository on GitHub first, with the README ticked this once, then open it with Code → Codespaces → Create codespace on main — the repository is cloned and authenticated for you, and every later session runs in that codespace.)

docs.title: 7. Cheat sheet
docs.text: Command What it does git init Start tracking the current folder (creates .git) git status What is modified, staged, untracked — run it constantly git add <file> / git add . Put a file / everything on the staging area git commit -m "message" Seal the staging area into a snapshot git log --oneline / --graph --all The history, one line per commit / drawn, all branches git diff / git diff --staged Unstaged / staged changes against the last commit git show <hash> Message and diff of one commit git restore <file> Discard uncommitted edits (no undo!) git restore --staged <file> Take a file off the staging area, keep the edit git restore --source=<hash> <file> Get a file's content from an old commit git branch / git branch -a List local branches / including the remote's git switch -c <name> / git switch <name> Create-and-go / go to a branch git merge <name> Merge a branch into the current one (fast-forward or merge commit) git merge --abort Give up on a conflicted merge, back to before git branch -d <name> Delete a merged branch's pointer git clone <url> Copy a remote repository to your machine git remote -v / git remote add <name> <url> List remotes / add one git push -u origin main / git push Send commits up (first time / afterwards) git pull Bring remote commits down

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Full statements, expected outputs and solutions on the exercises page. Tags: [core] in class · [stretch] if you are ahead · [home] after class.

  1. [core] Recipe history — clone KnuxV/recipe-history, read eight commits like a detective, restore one quantity without losing what came after. First contact with git clone and git remote -v.
  2. [core] Scrabble counter: three merges — clone KnuxV/scrabble-counter: one branch fast-forwards, one makes a merge commit, one conflicts. Resolve it by hand.
  3. [core] Your course repository — section 6. The deliverable.
  4. [stretch] Keep a trace: fork or second remote — put your exercise work on your own GitHub, either by forking first or by adding a second remote to your clone.
  5. [home] Reading — Session 1½ — Git as a collaboration tool.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
1. Pro Git, 2nd ed. (Chacon & Straub, free) — read §2 "Git Basics" and §3.1–3.2 only; it is the reference, not a beginner's book.
  2. Learn Git Branching — interactive commit-graph visualiser; the fastest way to make "a branch is a pointer" click.
  3. Software Carpentry — Version Control with Git — the novice curriculum for researchers this session's pacing follows.
  4. Oh Shit, Git!?! — recovery recipes; exactly what you need after an agent commits garbage.
  5. Ambitious: GitHub Skills — Introduction to GitHub (hands-on, ~1h, automated feedback), then How to Write a Git Commit Message — the norms you will ask your agent to follow.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
By the end of the two hours you can:

  1. explain what pip, a virtual environment and a requirements.txt are — the classic toolkit you will meet in every existing project — and what they leave out;
  2. create a Python project with uv — pinned interpreter, declared dependencies, lockfile — and explain what each of the three files is for;
  3. turn a notebook cell with hard-coded values into a script with command-line arguments (argparse), run it with uv run, and get --help for free;
  4. install someone else's project in one command (uv sync), fork it, and extend its command line on a branch;
  5. explain what an environment variable is, store a secret for good — in ~/.bashrc or in a .env file — read it from Python, and say why it never goes in code;
  6. (bonus) read a CSV with Polars and do a group-by in five lines.

Deliverable: a reproducible script committed to your course repository — pyproject.toml, uv.lock, .python-version, report.py — and UNISTRA_API_KEY surviving a new terminal. The second item is Session 3's prerequisite; without it, Session 3 begins with a 401.

docs.title: Before class
docs.text:
• Your course repository from Session 1 exists on GitHub and on your machine.
  • Your Unistra API key is stored as an environment variable (setup, section 5). Test in a new terminal: echo $UNISTRA_API_KEY | cut -c1-6 prints sk-XXX.
  • Ten minutes of reading: uv — Working on projects, sections Creating a new project to Managing dependencies.
  • Five minutes: the README of github.com/KnuxV/password-generator, the project you will fork in class.
  • You do not need to install Python. uv installs the exact version the project asks for, by itself. (Section 2 uses whatever python3 your machine already has, if any; python3 --version tells you.)

docs.title: 1. Why: "it works on my machine" is not a result
docs.text:
Your workflow so far is Colab: open a browser, get a machine with some Python and some packages, run cells until the table appears. Which Python? Which pandas? Whatever Google installed that month. Re-run the notebook next year and the numbers may differ, or the code may not run at all — and you will not know which of the two hundred libraries changed.

For a scientist that is not an inconvenience, it is a validity problem. A result nobody can reproduce, including you in six months, is a claim, not a finding. Journals and data editors now require the replication package to pin its environment (the optional replication track is built on exactly this). Three things must be fixed for a Python project to be reproducible:

Layer Question Answered by The interpreter Which Python? 3.12, not "whatever python is" .python-version The direct dependencies Which libraries did I ask for? pyproject.toml The exact resolved set Which exact versions of those, and of everything they pull in? uv.lock

Python's classic answer to these questions is a trio of tools — pip, venv, requirements.txt — that you will meet in every project written before 2024 and in most tutorials, so section 2 shows them first. From section 3 on we use uv, one tool that does the same job, completely, faster, on every platform.

docs.title: 2. The classic toolkit: pip, venv, requirements.txt
docs.text: Read this section on any machine; type it if python3 --version prints a version (WSL, Mac, Codespaces). Git Bash users: read along — there is no Python on your machine yet, and that is one of the things uv fixes in section 3.

docs.title: 2.1 pip install and the one-Python problem
docs.text:
Python ships with a package installer, pip. pip install polars downloads polars from PyPI (the Python Package Index, the public catalogue every import you have ever typed came from) and copies it into the Python that ran pip. Colab does exactly this when a cell says !pip install something.

On your own machine the trouble starts with the word the. There is one Python, and every project installs into it. Your thesis needs pandas 1.5; a tutorial you follow next week installs pandas 2.3 on top; the thesis code now breaks, and six months later you cannot say which of the two hundred packages in that Python your thesis actually used. The system Python on Ubuntu and macOS is also used by the operating system itself, which is why pip install there is refused outright on recent versions (externally-managed-environment).

docs.title: 2.2 A virtual environment: one Python per project
docs.text:
The fix, since 2012, is the virtual environment: a folder inside the project that holds a private Python and its own packages. Make one by hand, once, to see what it is:

Ubuntu window, Terminal (Mac), or Codespace terminal
mkdir ~/venv-demo
cd ~/venv-demo
python3 -m venv .venv
ls -a
ls .venv/bin

python3 -m venv .venv creates the folder .venv (the name is a convention). Inside, bin/ holds a python, a pip, and a script called activate. Nothing is installed yet. (On WSL, if this complains about ensurepip, Ubuntu ships Python without that piece: sudo apt install python3-venv, then retry.)

Now activate it:

Same terminal, inside venv-demo
source .venv/bin/activate
which python
pip install polars
python -c "import polars; print(polars.__version__)"

Three things to notice. Your prompt now starts with (.venv). which python answers /home/you/venv-demo/.venv/bin/python — the private one, not /usr/bin/python3. And pip install polars therefore went into .venv, nowhere else. Activation is nothing magical: activate puts .venv/bin at the front of your PATH for this window, so that python and pip resolve to the private copies.

Prove the isolation, then leave:

Same terminal
deactivate
which python
python3 -c "import polars"

After deactivate the prompt is back to normal, which python is the system Python again (or nothing), and the import fails with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'polars': polars exists only inside venv-demo/.venv. That is the whole idea — one environment per project, and the project's folder is the unit of reproducibility.

For recognition only: on Windows (outside WSL) the scripts live in .venv\Scripts\ instead of .venv/bin/, so tutorials say .venv\Scripts\activate. Same thing.

docs.title: 2.3 requirements.txt: the list you ship
docs.text:
An environment is not shareable — it is a folder full of compiled files for your machine — but the list of what is in it is. The convention is a text file, requirements.txt, one package per line, produced by pip freeze:

Same terminal, inside venv-demo
source .venv/bin/activate
pip freeze > requirements.txt
cat requirements.txt
deactivate

polars==1.44.1
polars-runtime-32==1.44.1

Whoever receives the project runs the three-line ritual you will find in thousands of READMEs — create, activate, install from the list:

The recipient's side (do not run it now)
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

You have now seen every piece of the classic toolkit: pip installs, venv isolates, requirements.txt transmits.

docs.title: 2.4 What is still missing
docs.text:
Look at the two lines of requirements.txt against the three-layer table of section 1:

  • Which Python? Not in the file. The recipient's python3 may be 3.9 or 3.14; polars 1.44 may not even install on one of them.
  • What did I ask for? You asked for polars; polars-runtime-32 came along with it. pip freeze flattens direct and indirect dependencies into one list, so a year later nobody knows which lines can be removed.
  • Is it really the same file? Version numbers, no checksums. Rare, but a package can be re-uploaded under the same version.
  • Three commands and a trap. "Did you activate?" is the most common support question in any Python course: (.venv) is missing from the prompt, python is the system one, and the error is No module named polars although you installed it — into the other Python.

uv keeps the good idea (the .venv folder — the same folder, with the same layout) and fixes the four gaps: the Python version is pinned in a file, your direct dependencies are declared in pyproject.toml, the exact resolved set with hashes is written to uv.lock, and activation is done for you on every command. The rest of the session is that. Clean up first:

Any terminal
cd ~
rm -rf ~/venv-demo
Classic uv (sections 3–4) python3 -m venv .venv uv venv — or nothing: uv run creates it when needed source .venv/bin/activate then python x.py uv run x.py pip install polars uv add polars pip freeze > requirements.txt uv.lock, written automatically pip install -r requirements.txt uv sync

docs.title: 3. Install uv
docs.text:
WSL (Ubuntu) / Mac / CodespacesGit Bash Ubuntu window, Terminal (Mac), or Codespace terminal
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

uv is a Windows program here; install it from PowerShell, then use it from Git Bash.

Windows PowerShell (NOT administrator)
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

If you installed Scoop during setup, scoop install main/uv works too. TODO(verify): confirm on a Windows laptop that Git Bash finds uv after a new window (the installer adds it to the Windows user PATH; Git Bash inherits it).

The installer puts uv in ~/.local/bin and adds that folder to your PATH — for future terminals. So, the ritual you learned in Session 0: close the terminal, open a new one, then:

Any terminal — new window
uv --version

Expected: uv 0.12.x (any 0.12 or later is fine). Commands checked against uv — Installation.

docs.title: 4.1 uv init
docs.text:
Go into your course repository and initialise a project in place (no folder name after init; the project takes the folder's name):

Any terminal
cd ~/agent-lab
uv init --no-package --python 3.12
ls -a

Two flags, both deliberate:

  • --python 3.12 pins the interpreter. Without it, uv picks the newest Python it can find — different on every laptop, and your lockfiles would disagree with your neighbour's and with Codespaces.
  • --no-package gives the simple layout: one main.py at the top. (Since uv 0.12 the default is a src/ package layout with a build system — right for libraries, noise for us.)

Expected files (plus your .git, README.md and .gitignore from Session 1):

.python-version   pyproject.toml   main.py
  • .python-version contains 3.12. Every uv command in this folder uses that Python — downloading it first if needed.
  • pyproject.toml is the project's declaration: name, the Python requirement, and an empty dependencies = [] list. This is the standard file every Python tool reads.
  • main.py is a hello-world.

uv init inside an existing git repository

uv notices the .git you created in Session 1 and does not create a second one. It also does not write a .gitignore in that case — which is why Session 1 made you write one with .venv/ in it.

docs.title: 4.2 uv run — the environment appears
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv run main.py
ls -a

The first run prints a few lines — Using CPython 3.12.x, Creating virtual environment at: .venv — then Hello from agent-lab!. A new folder .venv exists. That is the virtual environment of section 2.2 — the very same kind of folder: ls .venv/bin shows the same activate, python and pip, and packages will land in the same place. Two differences. It holds a private Python 3.12, the version pinned in .python-version, whatever python3 your machine has (or has not). And you never activate it by hand: uv run <something> means "run this with the project's .venv", so the "did you activate?" trap of section 2.4 disappears. (If a tutorial insists, source .venv/bin/activate works on a uv-made environment too; deactivate leaves it.)

.venv is machine-specific and large. It is never committed — it is in your .gitignore, and uv also drops a .gitignore inside it as a belt-and-braces. Anyone who clones your repo recreates it in seconds from the lockfile (section 4.4).

docs.title: 4.3 uv add — declare a dependency
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv add polars
cat pyproject.toml
ls -a

Three things happened:

  1. pyproject.toml now says dependencies = ["polars>=1.44.1"] — what you asked for, with a lower bound.
  2. A new file, uv.lock, lists the exact version of polars and of everything polars depends on, with a cryptographic hash of each downloaded file. Open it (head -20 uv.lock); you will never edit it by hand, but you will always commit it.
  3. Polars was installed into .venv.

Check it works:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv run python -c "import polars; print(polars.__version__)"

Expected: 1.44.1 (or later, if you add it after this page was written). To remove a dependency: uv remove polars. To see the tree: uv tree.

pyproject.toml is the wish, uv.lock is the receipt

The first says "I need polars, at least 1.44". The second says "on 18 September 2026 that resolved to polars 1.44.1, polars-runtime-32 1.44.1, these exact files". Both are committed; the receipt is what makes the result reproducible next year.

docs.title: 4.4 uv sync — reproduce it elsewhere
docs.text:
This is the other half of the story. On any other machine (a classmate's laptop, a Codespace, the university cluster):

Any terminal
git clone https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/agent-lab.git
cd agent-lab
uv sync

uv sync reads .python-version and uv.lock, fetches that exact Python if missing, and rebuilds .venv identically. Same numbers, guaranteed by hashes. (uv run does this implicitly too; uv sync is the explicit form you put in a README.) This is the one-line replacement for the three-line ritual of section 2.3, and it is how you will install the password generator in exercise 2.3.

A project that only has a requirements.txt

Older projects have no pyproject.toml or uv.lock, only the frozen list. uv reads it: inside the cloned folder, uv init --no-package --python 3.12 then uv add -r requirements.txt turns every line into a declared dependency and writes the lockfile; from then on, uv run and uv sync as usual. (There is also uv pip install -r requirements.txt, a drop-in for pip that installs into .venv without declaring anything — fine for a one-off, not for a project you keep.)

docs.title: 4.5 Commit the project files
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside agent-lab
git status
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version main.py
git commit -m "Initialise uv project with polars"
git push

git status must not list .venv — if it does, your .gitignore is missing the .venv/ line; add it before committing.

docs.title: 5. From a notebook cell to a script with arguments
5.1 The gap this session closes
docs.text:
In a notebook, a parameter is a variable you edit at the top of the cell and re-run:

What it looks like in Colab
import polars as pl

CSV_FILE = "sales.csv"      # edit here…
TOP = 3                     # …and here, then Shift+Enter

df = pl.read_csv(CSV_FILE)
result = (
    df.with_columns((pl.col("units") * pl.col("unit_price")).alias("revenue"))
    .group_by("region")
    .agg(pl.col("revenue").sum())
    .sort("revenue", descending=True)
    .head(TOP)
)
result

That works for one person, once. It cannot be run on ten files in a loop, scheduled every night, called by a colleague who does not open notebooks, or — in Session 4 — called by an agent that needs to test your code. The industry form of the same thing is a script with arguments: uv run report.py sales.csv --top 3. The values that used to be "edit the cell" are now typed on the command line.

Get the toy data (nine rows, invented; columns region, product, units, unit_price):

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
curl -LO https://knuxv.github.io/cours-agents/files/sales.csv
head -3 sales.csv

docs.title: 5.2 The script
docs.text:
Create report.py with the following content (nano report.py, paste, Ctrl+O, Enter, Ctrl+X — or VS Code). Also downloadable: report.py.

report.py
"""Total revenue per region from a sales CSV. Usage: uv run report.py sales.csv --top 2"""
import argparse
import polars as pl


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Revenue per region from a sales CSV.")
    parser.add_argument("csv_file", help="path to the CSV (columns: region, product, units, unit_price)")
    parser.add_argument("--top", type=int, default=3, help="how many regions to show (default: 3)")
    parser.add_argument("--product", help="keep only this product (default: all)")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    df = pl.read_csv(args.csv_file)
    if args.product:
        df = df.filter(pl.col("product") == args.product)
    result = (
        df.with_columns((pl.col("units") * pl.col("unit_price")).alias("revenue"))
        .group_by("region")
        .agg(pl.col("revenue").sum())
        .sort("revenue", descending=True)
        .head(args.top)
    )
    print(result)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Read it top to bottom; four ideas carry the whole of argparse:

  • A parser describes what the command accepts. The description shows up in --help.
  • A positional argument (csv_file) is required and identified by its position: report.py sales.csv.
  • An option (--top, --product) starts with --, is optional, and can have a default and a type. type=int converts the text "2" to the number 2 and rejects "two" with a clean error.
  • parse_args() returns an object; args.top is your old TOP variable. The rest of the function is the notebook cell, unchanged, with the two constants replaced.

The if __name__ == "__main__": line means "run main() only when this file is executed as a script, not when it is imported". You will see it in every Python script from now on; type it, do not question it yet.

docs.title: 5.3 Run it
docs.text:
Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv run report.py sales.csv --top 2

Expected:

shape: (2, 2)
┌──────────┬─────────┐
│ region   ┆ revenue │
│ ---      ┆ ---     │
│ str      ┆ f64     │
╞══════════╪═════════╡
│ Bretagne ┆ 937.5   │
│ Alsace   ┆ 828.5   │
└──────────┴─────────┘

Now the things you got for free:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv run report.py --help
uv run report.py sales.csv --product tea
uv run report.py
uv run report.py sales.csv --top two
  • --help prints a usage message built from your help= strings — documentation that cannot drift from the code.
  • The third command fails with error: the following arguments are required: csv_file, the fourth with argument --top: invalid int value: 'two', both with exit code 2 and no Python traceback. Input validation, without writing any.

Commit:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
git add report.py sales.csv
git commit -m "Add revenue report script with argparse"
git push

Deeper: Python HOWTO — Argparse Tutorial (official, incremental) and last year's complete class guide (sys.argv, flags, choices, mutually exclusive groups — well past what you need this week).

docs.title: 6.1 What they are
docs.text:
Every program you start receives a small dictionary of named values from the shell that started it: the environment. Some are set by the system (HOME, your home folder; PATH, the folders searched for commands); any you like can be added. Look at yours:

Any terminal
echo $HOME
echo $PATH
env | head -5

$NAME reads a variable in the shell. Set one for this window only:

Any terminal
export GREETING="bonjour"
echo $GREETING

Open a second terminal window and run echo $GREETING there: empty. export affects the current shell and the programs it launches, nothing else. To make a variable exist in every future window, the line goes in the shell's startup file — ~/.bashrc on WSL, Codespaces and Git Bash, ~/.zshrc on a Mac — which is exactly what setup section 5.2 had you do for UNISTRA_API_KEY. Confirm it took, in a new window:

Any terminal — new window
echo $UNISTRA_API_KEY | cut -c1-6

If that prints an empty line, fix it now (wrong file, or the terminal was not reopened); Session 3 depends on it.

docs.title: 6.2 Reading them from Python
docs.text:
whoami.py
import os

key = os.environ.get("UNISTRA_API_KEY")
if key is None:
    raise SystemExit("UNISTRA_API_KEY is not set. See the setup page, section 5.")
print("key found, starts with", key[:6])
Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv run whoami.py

Expected: key found, starts with sk-XXX. os.environ is the environment as a dictionary; .get() returns None instead of crashing when the name is absent, so the script can fail with a sentence rather than a KeyError traceback. Failing loudly and early on a missing secret is the correct behaviour — an agent reading that message knows what to do; one reading a traceback guesses.

docs.title: 6.3 Two homes for a secret: ~/.bashrc or .env
docs.text:
The key has to live somewhere on disk, or you would type it at every run. Two places are legitimate; you have used the first, and many projects you clone will expect the second.

Home A — the shell's startup file. What setup section 5.2 did: one export UNISTRA_API_KEY="sk-XXXX" line in ~/.bashrc (or ~/.zshrc). Scope: you, on this machine, in every terminal and every project. Nothing to add to any repository. Right for a personal key you use everywhere — and it is what curl will read in Session 3, so keep it.

Home B — a .env file in the project folder. A plain text file named exactly .env, one NAME=value per line, no export, no spaces around =:

.env — inside agent-lab (create it with nano or VS Code)
UNISTRA_API_KEY=sk-XXXX

Scope: this project, for whoever runs it — a classmate, a Codespace, a CI job, a Docker container, an agent. The project declares which variables it needs; each copy of the project supplies its own values. Python does not read .env by itself; the python-dotenv package does, and it is a dependency like any other:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv add python-dotenv
whoami.py — the .env-aware version
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv()  # reads .env in the current folder, if there is one

key = os.environ.get("UNISTRA_API_KEY")
if key is None:
    raise SystemExit("UNISTRA_API_KEY is not set. See the setup page, section 5.")
print("key found, starts with", key[:6])

load_dotenv() copies each line of .env into os.environ, and the rest of the script is unchanged: it still reads the environment, it does not know or care where the value came from. A variable that already exists in the shell wins over the file (load_dotenv does not override), so Home A and Home B coexist without surprise.

Now the part that matters. .env is never committed. Your .gitignore from Session 1 already has the line; check that Git really ignores the file, then look at git status:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
git check-ignore -v .env
git status

Expected: .gitignore:2:.env .env — the rule, its line number, the file — and a git status in which .env does not appear (whoami.py, pyproject.toml and uv.lock do; commit those). If .env shows up as untracked, add the line: echo ".env" >> .gitignore. The convention for telling others which variables to fill in is a second file, .env.example, with the names and placeholder values, which is committed:

.env.example — committed
UNISTRA_API_KEY=sk-XXXX

Which home for the course? Keep A — Session 3's curl commands need the shell variable. Add B the day you share or deploy a project, and you will recognise it in every repository that ships a .env.example.

docs.title: 6.4 Why the key never goes in the code
docs.text:
Three reasons, in increasing order of seriousness.

  1. Configuration is not code. The same script runs with your key on your laptop, with a colleague's on theirs, with a test key in CI. Hard-coding it means editing the code to change who runs it. (The Twelve-Factor App — Config, two paragraphs, is the canonical statement.)
  2. Git remembers forever. You learned in Session 1 that a commit is permanent. A key pasted in report.py, committed, then deleted in the next commit is still in the history, and git log -p shows it to anyone with the repository. Bots scan public GitHub for sk- strings within minutes of a push.
  3. Agents copy what they see. In Session 4 an agent will read your files to work on them. A key in the code ends up in its context, its logs, and possibly its next commit.

So: the secret lives in the environment — put there by ~/.bashrc or by a .env file that Git ignores; the code reads os.environ; the repository contains the name of the variable (in the README, or in .env.example), never its value. A .env file committed "just this once" is exactly reason 2: it is in the history for good.

If a key was ever committed

Deleting it from the file does nothing. Regenerate the key (setup 5.1) so the leaked one is worthless, then fix the repository. Come and see us; rewriting history is possible but is not a beginner operation.

docs.title: 7. Bonus: Polars in five minutes
docs.text:
You already used it in report.py. Polars is a DataFrame library like pandas, written in Rust: much faster, stricter about types, and built around expressions — pl.col("units") * pl.col("unit_price") describes a computation, and Polars runs it in an optimised plan — instead of pandas' chained indexing. Coming from pandas, the three habits to relearn:

pandas Polars df[df["product"] == "tea"] df.filter(pl.col("product") == "tea") df["revenue"] = df["units"] * df["unit_price"] df.with_columns((pl.col("units") * pl.col("unit_price")).alias("revenue")) df.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum() df.group_by("region").agg(pl.col("revenue").sum())

Try it live:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
uv run python -c "import polars as pl; df = pl.read_csv('sales.csv'); print(df.describe())"

Read next: Polars — Coming from pandas. The stretch exercise times the two libraries on a larger file.

docs.title: 8. The deliverable, checked
docs.text:
In your course repository:

Any terminal, inside agent-lab
git status                                   # working tree clean, .venv not listed
ls pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version report.py sales.csv
uv run report.py sales.csv --top 2           # the table above
git log --oneline | head -3                  # your Session 2 commits, pushed

And in a new terminal window:

Any terminal — new window
uv --version
echo $UNISTRA_API_KEY | cut -c1-6

Both must print something. A script that runs these checks for you (check-setup.sh) will be linked here once ready — TODO(verify): Task 03.

docs.title: 9. When things go wrong
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix uv: command not found right after installing PATH is read when a terminal starts Open a new terminal. Still nothing on WSL/Mac: source ~/.bashrc (or ~/.zshrc) uv init says a pyproject.toml already exists You ran it twice Nothing to do python3 -m venv fails with ensurepip is not available (WSL) Ubuntu ships Python without venv sudo apt install python3-venv, retry pip install refused: externally-managed-environment You are installing into the system Python Activate a virtual environment first — or use uv add (.venv) not in the prompt, No module named X although you installed it Environment not activated; python is the system one source .venv/bin/activate — or uv run, which never has this problem Your uv.lock differs from a classmate's for the same pyproject.toml Different Python pinned Both check cat .python-version; it must say 3.12 No module named polars You ran python report.py instead of uv run report.py Always uv run git status shows hundreds of files under .venv .gitignore missing .venv/ echo ".venv/" >> .gitignore, then git status again echo $UNISTRA_API_KEY is empty in a new window Line went in the wrong startup file, or the window is not new echo $SHELL; bash → ~/.bashrc, zsh → ~/.zshrc; redo setup 5.2 .env exists but Python says the variable is not set load_dotenv() not called, or .env is in another folder (it reads the current directory) ls -a in the folder you run from; the file is named exactly .env git status lists .env .gitignore is missing the line echo ".env" >> .gitignore. If it was already committed: see the red box in section 6.4 Failed to hardlink files; falling back to full copy warning Cache and project on different drives (e.g. work kept under /mnt/c in WSL) Harmless. Better: keep projects in ~ — see where to keep your work Arguments with spaces or * behave oddly Shell quoting Quote them: --product "green tea"

docs.title: 10. Cheat sheet
docs.text: Command What it does uv init --no-package --python 3.12 New project in the current folder, flat layout, Python pinned uv add <pkg> / uv remove <pkg> Declare / undeclare a dependency (updates pyproject.toml and uv.lock) uv run <script.py> [args] Run inside the project's environment (creates it if needed) uv sync Rebuild .venv exactly from uv.lock uv tree Show installed packages and their dependencies uv python install 3.12 Fetch a Python version (usually implicit) export NAME="value" Set a variable for this window echo 'export NAME="value"' >> ~/.bashrc …for every future window (~/.zshrc on Mac) echo $NAME / env Read one / all variables os.environ.get("NAME") Read it from Python (None if unset) load_dotenv() (package python-dotenv) Also read a .env file in the current folder into the environment python3 -m venv .venv / source .venv/bin/activate / deactivate Classic: create / enter / leave a virtual environment by hand pip install -r requirements.txt / pip freeze > requirements.txt Classic: install from / write the frozen list (uv sync / uv.lock do this)

  1. [core] A uv project from scratch — sections 4.1–4.5 in your course repo; done when a classmate can git clone it and uv sync without errors.
  2. [core] Notebook → script — section 5 with report.py, then add a third argument of your choice (e.g. --region to filter by region, or --csv to print CSV instead of a table).
  3. [core] Fork and extend the password generator — fork KnuxV/password-generator, uv sync, read its argparse command line with us, then add --separator and --numbers on two branches.
  4. [home] Secret hygiene audit — a provided repository in which an API key was committed, then "removed". Find it in the history, list every place it leaked, write the two commands that would have prevented it. TODO(verify): starter repo published with the exercises of Task 03.
  5. [stretch] Polars vs pandas — load a larger CSV with both, time the same group-by, and write three lines on the difference in how you express the computation, not just the speed.

docs.title: Going further
docs.text:
1. uv docs — Working on projects — init/add/run/lock/sync on one page.
  2. Python docs — venv and Installing packages with pip — the classic toolkit, from the source; last year's lesson walks through it at class pace.
  3. Python HOWTO — Argparse Tutorial — official, incremental, exactly the notebook→script scope.
  4. The Twelve-Factor App — Config — the two paragraphs that settle "why environment variables"; python-dotenv — README for the .env conventions.
  5. Polars — Coming from pandas — the bridge for this audience.
  6. Ambitious: The Missing Semester — Shell Tools and Scripting — variables, $(), scripts, ~/.bashrc: from "I run commands" to "I automate them".
